title: Nestorius and Cyril on the Title of Mary
english: Nestorius says: When the divine Scripture speaks of Christ's birth from Mary the Virgin, or of his death, it is nowhere found to use the name 'God', but 'Christ' or 'Lord' or 'Jesus', since these three names point to the two natures, sometimes to the one, sometimes to the other. Here is what I mean: when the Apostle makes known to us Christ's birth from the Virgin, he says, 'God sent forth his own Son, born of a woman' (Galatians 4:4); he did not say, 'He sent forth God the Word.' He takes instead the name that points to the two births, that is, God and man, since Christ is twofold. For the Virgin bore a son of God, just as he said, 'You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High' (Psalm 82:6). Hence we have learned from Scripture to say 'Christ-bearer' (Christotokos), 'Lord-bearer' and 'man-bearer'; but we were never taught to call the holy Virgin 'God-bearer' (Theotokos).
Cyril says: Isaiah cries out in the Spirit: 'Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel' (Isaiah 7:14), which is…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76, cols. 249-252 (Dialogus cum Nestorio). The heading of the print, 'Dialogue of the same holy Cyril with Nestorius, that the holy Virgin is God-bearer and not Christ-bearer', and the column numbers are not part of the reading text.

The bracketed [ἢ] before θάνατον is the editor's supplied 'or', and is translated: 'or of his death'. The other bracketed readings ([ξοδ. μηνύων], [ξοδ. Θεὸς]) are editorial variants that do not change the sense.
καθότι ἔφησεν is 'just as he said', introducing Psalm 82:6 (LXX 81:6), which Nestorius quotes to show that 'son of God' can be said of men.

The Isaiah quotation reads 'they will call', the form found in Matthew 1:23; it is cited to Isaiah 7:14, the prophet Cyril names. The sentence breaks off at 'which is' and continues at the start of the next section ('translated, God with us').
